title: SA renews global showcase deal with Bordeaux wine museum
summary:
South Australian wines will continue to be showcased at La Cité du Vin, a prestigious wine museum in France, following a new two-year deal signed by the state government. Attracting more than 3.5 million visitors from across the world since it was established a decade ago, La Cité du Vin “delivers immersive showcases of the world’s best wines”. content:
South Australian wines will continue to be showcased at La Cité du Vin, a prestigious wine museum in France, following a new two-year deal signed by the state government.

Attracting more than 3.5 million visitors from across the world since it was established a decade ago, La Cité du Vin “delivers immersive showcases of the world’s best wines”.

The new Memorandum of Understanding between the SA government and the wine museum in Bordeaux was signed on the eve of the Great Wine Capitals Global Network’s International Annual Conference, which is currently underway in Hawke’s Bay, New Zealand.

Through this renewed partnership, South Australian winemakers will showcase their wines through tastings in the museum’s Belvedere Room, “against a 360-degree panoramic backdrop of Bordeaux”.

South Australian wine producers will also host special events and deliver tasting masterclasses at the museum.

Clare Scriven MLC, Minister for Primary Industries and Regional Development, said the deal secures SA’s place in the world’s most prestigious wine museum.

“South Australia is home to an extraordinary wine industry, with iconic producers with global reputations and emerging winemakers who are working hard to make their mark around the world.

“Partnerships like this help South Australia share its story with new audiences, build new connections between local producers and international consumers, and support the long-term growth of our wine and tourism industries,” Minister Scriven said.

Florence Maffrand, head of wine partnerships & international patronage at La Cite du Vin, said they are delighted to continue the partnership.

“Since 2016, the mission of the Foundation for wine culture and civilisations has been to share the universal heritage of wine with visitors to La Cité du Vin. We want to spark curiosity, encourage discovery and, above all, make visitors want to go further, to continue this journey elsewhere.

“Our wine partners are at the heart of what we offer; they are truly indispensable. Wines are essential to creating experiences with our audiences: they allow us to deepen our understanding of wine cultures around the world,” Maffrand said.

Minister for Tourism Emily Bourke added that the venue provides incredible exposure for SA wineries, with nearly 400,000 people visiting the museum last year.

“Initiatives like this and South Australia’s recent success in the Michelin Guide, with 77 restaurants now featured in the global culinary bible, reinforces our state’s growing reputation as a must-visit destination for world-class wine and food.”

The state has been showcasing its wine at the institution since 2017, with forty SA wine producers having been showcased at La Cité du Vin to date.

Jo Collins, Great Wine Capitals Global Network president, said the partnership renewal is an important investment in the global recognition of SA’s wine industry and the people behind it.

“Through our collaboration with the museum, we can showcase our exceptional wine producers to international audiences, share the stories behind our world-class wine regions and continue to strengthen Adelaide’s profile as a globally competitive wine and tourism destination.

“This partnership creates valuable opportunities to celebrate South Australia’s wine excellence on the world stage, and we look forward to continuing our work with the museum to raise the profile of our wine producers and regions internationally.”

The SA government shared that the collaboration has also enabled a portrait of Munda Wines owner and founder Pauly Vandenbergh to be featured at La Cité du Vin’s international photography exhibition, which is currently open to the public until the end of the year.

South Australia produces 80 per cent of Australia’s premium wine and 50 per cent of all bottled wine. The sector supports more than 90,000 jobs, includes almost 700 wineries and more than 70,000 hectares of vines.

The post Audit reveals just 8.7% of wines served in NSW government owned buildings are local appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
An audit of 29 restaurant and bar wine lists at venues in NSW government owned buildings has found that of 2,181 wines, just 189 or 8.7% were from NSW.

Conducted by David Cumming, director of Define Wine Marketing & Communications and owner of The Lane Cellars in Orange, the audit counted every wine on each venue’s most recently published list by region and was read between July and October 2026. Venues without a publicly available list were excluded.

The audit found only one venue exclusively pours NSW wine at its events — the International Convention Centre Sydney (ICC) at Darling Harbour.

Cumming shared that adding the ICC’s 100 NSW wines to the total is enough to skew it majorly, making the figure rise to 289 of 2,281 wines or 12.7%. Including that one venue in the total would account for more than a third of all NSW wine counted.

At the new Sydney Fish Market, Cumming found that seven restaurants publish 441 wines between them and just 33 (7.5%) of those are from NSW.

“There are three times as many South Australian wines on those lists as NSW wines, and three times as many French wines,” he said.

The Centennial Homestead is a similar story, with only six of 50 wines being from NSW.

He found that some lists have no NSW wine at all, such as The Observer Hotel with its 17 wines.

Cumming added that Eternity Bar at Central Station opened in 2018 “promising a focus on NSW wine”, however, its latest published list has 11 wines, and none are from NSW. At Manly Pavilion, on Transport for NSW land, three of 67 wines are from NSW.

“NSW is the only state where you can sit in a government-owned building, look out at the harbour, and struggle to find a wine from your own state,” said Cumming.

He highlighted that the flagship gallery restaurant in Perth pours 90 per cent Western Australian wine, whilst the Adelaide equivalent pours 71 per cent South Australian.

The issue was raised in NSW Parliament on 24 September 2026. Nationals MP for Monaro Nichole Overall asked Finance Minister Courtney Houssos what steps the government had taken to prioritise local wine in government owned, leased and contracted venues.

Cumming recalled the Minister’s answer pointed to the government’s Local Jobs First procurement legislation.

He says that misses the point and that “this is not a procurement issue”.

Because private operators, not the NSW government, buy wine at these venues, Cumming explained that the procurement rules do not reach them. Even if procurement did apply, he pointed out that the “local procurement legislation defines locally produced goods as anything made in Australia or New Zealand” rather than anything made in NSW.

“Parliament has been asked about government purchasing. Government isn’t the purchaser; government is the landlord. The landlord sets the terms of the lease — that is where the fix is,” Cumming said.

Following the question in Parliament, Cumming wrote to Arts Minister the Hon. John Graham MLC and Lands and Property Minister the Hon. Stephen Kamper MP.

He says the letters request that when a venue lease, licence or concession in a NSW government owned building is renewed or tendered, it should include a clause requiring a fair share of NSW wine on the list. Cumming proposed a baseline of 30 to 40 per cent and stressed that the change requires no new funding.

“Our winegrowers in Orange, Mudgee, the Hunter, Hilltops, Tumbarumba, the Riverina and Canberra District aren’t asking for a handout. They are asking for a place on the list in buildings the people of NSW already own,” he said.

There are a few venues which have reacted to the controversy, however.

Earlier in the year, the Art Gallery of NSW asked its caterer to review its NSW wine offerings and upped the count at its restaurant from three to eight. Since July, MOD Dining has listed 10 NSW wines out of 18, and the Gallery Café has four out of nine.

Meanwhile, the café at the Museum of Contemporary Art, which Cumming shared leases its Circular Quay building from Property NSW, already lists eight NSW wines out of 13. Winnie’s, which opened at the Sydney Opera House in August, lists 10 out of 14.

title: Barossa wine awarded a Wine Spectator Critics’ Choice Award for sixth time
summary:
First Drop Wines’ Mother’s Milk Shiraz, a wine that retails for just AUD $28, has been honoured with a Wine Spectator Critics’ Choice Award for the sixth time. The 2023 vintage will be recognised in New York City this Thursday, 22 October 2026, alongside many of the world’s most celebrated wines. Mother’s Milk has now been selected as a Critics’ Choice wine in 2016, 2017, 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 — including four consecutive years. “Each award comes from a different vintage, a different growing season and a fresh assessment by Wine Spectator’s editors. Winning once is a mark of quality; winning six times is proof of a wine that delivers, year after year,” the winery said.

content:
2026 is the sixth time it has been awarded with the honour. Image supplied

First Drop Wines’ Mother’s Milk Shiraz, a wine that retails for just AUD $28, has been honoured with a Wine Spectator Critics’ Choice Award for the sixth time.

The 2023 vintage will be recognised in New York City this Thursday, 22 October 2026, alongside many of the world’s most celebrated wines.

Mother’s Milk has now been selected as a Critics’ Choice wine in 2016, 2017, 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 — including four consecutive years.

“Each award comes from a different vintage, a different growing season and a fresh assessment by Wine Spectator’s editors. Winning once is a mark of quality; winning six times is proof of a wine that delivers, year after year,” the winery said.

Mother’s Milk was also named in Wine Spectator’s Top 100 Wines of the Year in back-to-back years — the 2020 vintage at number 26 in 2022 and the 2021 vintage at rank 38 in 2023 — and has “repeatedly featured in the magazine’s Top 100 Value Wines”.

The honour coincides with Wine Spectator’s 45th annual New York Wine Experience, held from 22 to 24 October at the New York Marriott Marquis in Times Square. The Critics’ Choice Grand Tastings, which are a part of the event, will be held on the evenings of Thursday 22 and Friday 23 October. The tastings will feature more than 250 wines rated 90-points or higher by Wine Spectator’s editors, poured by the winemakers themselves.

Winemaker and founder John Retsas said the sixth award was a validation of everything Mother’s Milk was created to be: “a wine of genuine quality that people can afford to enjoy, not just admire”.

“Six Critics’ Choice Awards is something we never imagined when we made the first vintage of Mother’s Milk.

“To be recognised once is an honour. To be recognised six times, across so many different vintages, tells us the wine is doing exactly what we set out to do — over-delivering on quality, vintage after vintage.

“Great wine shouldn’t be reserved for special occasions or deep pockets. Mother’s Milk is the elegance and generosity of the Barossa in a glass, and to stand alongside the world’s finest wines in New York for a sixth time is a credit to our team and our growers, who make this consistency possible,” Retsas said.

The 2023 Mother’s Milk Barossa Shiraz is sourced from vineyards across the Barossa Valley and Eden Valley and matured for 10 months in seasoned French oak hogsheads.

title: SA wine exporters fill the gap caused by US-Canada trade dispute
summary:
The South Australian Government has revealed that there has been a significant increase in sales of SA wine to Canada and that it will build on this momentum with a new trade official to be based in Canada. Nearly 18 months after several Canadian provinces pulled US wine from their shelves, Canada has emerged as a strong growth market, rising to become the state’s third largest wine export partner, overtaking the United States and behind only China and the United Kingdom. Following “swift and targeted investment by the state government and local winemakers”, wine exports to Canada have grown by over $24 million in the year to August 2026, now valued at $128 million.

The post SA wine exporters fill the gap caused by US-Canada trade dispute appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
The South Australian Government has revealed that there has been a significant increase in sales of SA wine to Canada and that it will build on this momentum with a new trade official to be based in Canada.

Nearly 18 months after several Canadian provinces pulled US wine from their shelves, Canada has emerged as a strong growth market, rising to become the state’s third largest wine export partner, overtaking the United States and behind only China and the United Kingdom.

Following “swift and targeted investment by the state government and local winemakers”, wine exports to Canada have grown by over $24 million in the year to August 2026, now valued at $128 million.

South Australia now accounts for 68 per cent of Australia’s total wine exports to Canada and exported 48.5 million litres of wine to Canada, up 38.6 per cent, in the year to August 2026.

Minister for State Development Chris Picton MP said the local wine industry quickly recognised an opportunity and moved quickly to get more wine on the shelves in Canada, “resulting in a major surge in sales through key Canadian retailers”.

“While the global wine market is undergoing a period of challenges and transition, it’s clear that South Australia remains well positioned for the future.

“By investing in these types of growth opportunities and leveraging the state’s unique ability to produce an exceptional diversity of quality wines, South Australia can continue to build a more sustainable and globally competitive future,” Minister Picton said.

Inca Lee, chief executive of the South Australian Wine Industry Association (SAWIA), said the result demonstrates both the global reputation of SA wine and the agility of local winemakers.

“The state government’s investment through the Global Wine Growth Program has ensured South Australian wineries are visible and competitive in Canada at a time when retailers are looking for alternatives and consumers are willing to try something new.

“We know global conditions remain challenging and competition for consumers is intense, which is why continued investment in export market development and diversification remains so important,” she said.

Beginning in March 2025, many Canadian provinces including Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia removed US alcoholic beverages from liquor outlets and online platforms in response to tariffs imposed by the US.

To further support South Australian export opportunities to Canada, recruitment will soon start for the new trade official position to be based in Toronto. The position aims to help South Australian trade and investment across the country in opportunities such as food, wine, critical minerals and defence. Canada was previously served from South Australian trade officials in the United States.

The SA government said it has supported a series of retail promotions throughout Canada, which have seen an uplift in South Australian wine sales across the largest retailers in the country.

Recently, a four-week in-store promotion was held with the LCBO during July and August, featuring 16 South Australian wines – including Angove, Zonte’s Footsteps, Kilikanoon, Two Hands, and Bleasdale – across nine flagship stores, “resulting in a 49 per cent uplift in sales during the promotional period”.

Vigneron and director of Zonte’s Footstep, Brad Rey, said Canada has become a focus for the winery.

“Canada is a key market for Zonte’s Footstep, and with the support and focus of the South Australian Government on building awareness of the diversity and quality of South Australia’s wines, it has become a focal point across many provincial markets.

“We have benefited from this support immensely, with trade and consumers supporting our wines and experiencing strong sales amid the global pressures our industry is experiencing.”

Additionally, more than 75 South Australian wine in-store tasting events were held at BCLDB locations throughout the Canadian summer months.

Canada is an increasingly important strategic economic partner and is the state’s eighth largest export market with total SA goods exports to Canada valued at $575 million, an increase of 4.4 per cent.

Minister Picton recently discussed the growing opportunities in Canada with Vic Fedeli, Ontario’s Minister for Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade, while both at a major defence conference in Poland.

content:
The Wine Industry Suppliers Association (WISA) has announced the finalists across six categories in the 2026 Wine Industry Impact Awards (WIIA). The finalists come from organisations whose products, services and partnerships are changing how Australian and New Zealand wine is grown, made, packaged and sold.

Winners will be revealed at the Wine Industry Impact Awards Gala Dinner on Thursday 19 November 2026 at The Playford Adelaide.

“This year’s finalists show that even in one of the toughest periods our industry has faced, innovative solutions to shared problems continue to thrive,” said Liz Schoen, executive chair for WISA.

“Suppliers haven’t stepped back because business is hard. They’ve kept investing in the growers and wineries they work with, and this year’s entrants are a testament to that resilience. From AI-driven business tools to on-vine yield sensors and sustainable packaging, every entry is solving a real problem for growers, winemakers and wine businesses.”

The finalists in each category are as follows:

The ‘Wine Australia’ Technology & Digital Innovation Award

  • BevSage — purpose-built AI combined with human expertise, giving wineries affordable access to commercial capability and market intelligence.
  • InnoVint (co-nominated with Hill Smith Family Estates) — a fast, low-disruption path off end-of-life production software, purpose-built for wineries.

The ‘SIG’ Winemaking & Oenology Award

  • Fermentis — the E2U yeast range, pitched directly into must without rehydration for safer, simpler fermentations.
  • Vason Group — X-PLANT® inactivated-yeast products supporting climate-resilient viticulture and winemaking.

The ‘Southern Premium Vineyards’ Viticulture & Grapegrowing Award

  • Ripen Tech — an on-vine system that measures grape bunch weight hourly for real-time yield monitoring.
  • Vason Group — X-PLANT® vineyard applications that help vines cope with heat and drought stress.
  • Affinity Labs — a Grapevine Clonal ID service that confirms clone identity before planting material reaches the vineyard.

The ‘MGA Insurance’ Sustainability Award

  • DeCam — affordable three-phase power for Southern Light Vineyards’ Long Gully Winery, ending its reliance on round-the-clock diesel generation.
  • Biogone — landfill-biodegradable packing tape, stretch wrap and shipping materials for moving wine.
  • Visy — major investment in glass beneficiation to lift recycled content in wine bottles.

The ‘Manheim Australia’ Packaging & Design Award

  • Australian Vintage — Poco Vino, a format-first brand in stylish 187ml single-serve bottles.
  • Amorim — Spark One Xpür®, the microplastic-free solution for sparkling wine

The Engineering & Equipment Award

  • Vinarchy (co-nominated with AWRI ) — autonomous GoTrack technology retrofitted to a conventional vineyard tractor, trialled at commercial scale.
  • Parsec by Enartis — EVO2FERM, predictive and adaptive yeast nutrition driven by real-time fermentation data.

content:
The estate is home to both Savannah Estate and LTA McGuigan Wines. Image supplied.

One of the Hunter Valley’s landmark tourism and hospitality estates, Blaxland Estate, has been put up for sale.

The property at 2198 Broke Road in Pokolbin consists of a 10.715-hectare landholding that is home to three established cellar door experiences, including Pokolbin Distillery, Savannah Estate and LTA McGuigan Wines, as well as the Blaxland Inn Restaurant.

The estate also has a detached accommodation residence and vineyards.

Blaxland Estate is located along Broke Road, one of the Hunter Valley’s key tourism routes, and sits in close proximity to major attractions such as Roche Estate, Brokenwood Wines and Hunter Valley Gardens.

It is being taken to the market via an expressions of interest campaign run by Knight Frank’s Brent Sinclair, in conjunction with Peter Dodds and Michael Chapman of Colliers.

Sinclair said Blaxland Estate presents a rare opportunity to secure a landmark landholding of scale in the heart of the Hunter Valley, combining diversified income, lifestyle appeal and significant future upside.

“Blaxland Estate is one of the Hunter Valley’s most recognisable tourism and hospitality properties, with a profile that extends well beyond the region itself,” he said.

“Properties of this scale and prominence rarely become available in Pokolbin, particularly those with an established income stream and a strategic landholding at the centre of Australia’s oldest wine region.

“The estate is surrounded by many of the Hunter Valley’s leading tourism attractions and hospitality operators, placing it in a position that is difficult to replicate.

“We expect the campaign to attract interest from private investors, family offices, tourism operators and high-net-worth groups seeking exposure to one of Australia’s most visited wine destinations,” he said.

Dodds said the Hunter Valley continues to benefit from strong tourism fundamentals with visitors drawn to the region’s wineries, events, food and accommodation offerings.

“Blaxland Estate provides investors with immediate holding income alongside the opportunity to secure a landmark property in a tightly held market where large-scale tourism assets seldom change hands.

“Given the property’s reputation, location and underlying landholding, we anticipate strong interest from both local and interstate purchasers.”

The expressions of interest campaign for Blaxland Estate will close at 3pm (AEDT) on 26 November.

title: New Zealand Winegrowers says India FTA opens new opportunities for local wine exporters
summary:
New Zealand Winegrowers (NZW) is celebrating the India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA) coming into force today, “bringing New Zealand wine improved access to one of the world’s fastest-growing economies”. NZW said the agreement gives New Zealand wine brands greater confidence to build their presence in India, with tariffs reducing progressively over the next decade. The FTA also includes a ‘Most Favoured Nation’ commitment for wine. If India agrees more favourable tariffs for wine in a future FTA with another country, eligible New Zealand wine will automatically receive the same tariff treatment. In addition, the FTA includes a dedicated ‘Annex on Trade in Wine, Whisky and Other Distilled Spirits’. NZW explained it aims to facilitate trade through “greater transparency, regulatory cooperation and clearer treatment of wine-specific issues” as well as establish “a working group on topics such as technical matters, labelling and certification”.

content:
India’s only MW, Sonal C Holland, presenting at the Wine Business Forum in Wellington. Image supplied

New Zealand Winegrowers (NZW) is celebrating the India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA) coming into force today, “bringing New Zealand wine improved access to one of the world’s fastest-growing economies”.

NZW said the agreement gives New Zealand wine brands greater confidence to build their presence in India, with tariffs reducing progressively over the next decade.

The FTA also includes a ‘Most Favoured Nation’ commitment for wine. If India agrees more favourable tariffs for wine in a future FTA with another country, eligible New Zealand wine will automatically receive the same tariff treatment. In addition, the FTA includes a dedicated ‘Annex on Trade in Wine, Whisky and Other Distilled Spirits’. NZW explained it aims to facilitate trade through “greater transparency, regulatory cooperation and clearer treatment of wine-specific issues” as well as establish “a working group on topics such as technical matters, labelling and certification”.

Improved access under the FTA is expected to make the market increasingly attractive to exporters. Depending on the wine’s value, tariffs on eligible New Zealand wine will reduce over ten years from 150% to either 50% or 25%.

New Zealand wine exports to India have “historically been modest, but they grew 48% in the last year to just under NZ$438,000”.

India’s wine market is largely concentrated in three cities: Mumbai, Delhi and Bengaluru. Together, those cities account for half of the country’s wine consumption and are home to around 70 million people. This is a market 13 times the size of New Zealand and is comparable to the United Kingdom.

Red wine accounts for a significant share of imported wine to India, “creating opportunities for a range of New Zealand wine styles alongside Sauvignon Blanc”. NZW said sales of wine are also growing. In the year to March 2026, Maharashtra (of which Mumbai is the capital city) sold a record 13 million litres, or around 1.4 million cases, while imports grew 14% by volume in 2025.

Together, the organisation believes these trends create a significant opportunity for New Zealand’s wine exporters.

“We thank Ministers and officials for their work to secure improved access to a market with considerable long-term potential”, said NZW CEO Anishka Jelicich.

“By working to bring the FTA into force quickly, the Government has ensured that New Zealand will also benefit from the Most Favoured Nation preferential tariff rates that have been negotiated under the EU India FTA. Those tariff reductions are more substantial and would not have been available to us if the EU deal had entered into force first.

“India remains largely untapped for New Zealand wine, so our focus is on helping our members assess the opportunity through practical market intelligence and insights, connections with key stakeholders and opportunities in-market to build their brands,” she said.

New Zealand Winegrowers recently hosted India’s only Master of Wine, Sonal C Holland, as a keynote speaker at its annual Wine Business Forum in Wellington. Her message to the audience was clear; the FTA removes a significant barrier, but long-term success in India will require commitment, patience and strong local relationships.

“Next month, we look forward to working with New Zealand Trade and Enterprise (NZTE) at ProWine Mumbai. The major international trade fair will include a 20 strong contingent of businesses showcasing New Zealand wine to the Indian trade. These types of events are incredibly valuable for our members, helping them to build distributor relationships and a pipeline in a growing premium segment,” said Jelicich.

title: Judging under way at the 2026 Marlborough Wine Show
summary:
More than 550 wines will be presented before the judges this week as tasting for the 2026 Marlborough Wine Show gets underway at Marlborough Events Centre. From Wednesday 21 to Friday 23 October, chief judge Stu Marfell will be joined by shadow chief judge Murray Cook to lead a team of ten senior judges and six associate judges, including guest judges Jennifer Docherty MW from Hong Kong and long-time international wine judge Terry Copeland, through the tasting. Entrants will be notified of medal results on Thursday 29 October, with trophy winners announced at the Marlborough Wine Show Celebration on Friday 13 November 2026.

The post Judging under way at the 2026 Marlborough Wine Show appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Entrants will be notified of medal results on Thursday 29 October and trophy winners announced Friday 13 November. Image supplied

More than 550 wines will be presented before the judges this week as tasting for the 2026 Marlborough Wine Show gets underway at Marlborough Events Centre.

From Wednesday 21 to Friday 23 October, chief judge Stu Marfell will be joined by shadow chief judge Murray Cook to lead a team of ten senior judges and six associate judges, including guest judges Jennifer Docherty MW from Hong Kong and long-time international wine judge Terry Copeland, through the tasting.

“We’re lucky to have two guest judges who bring real breadth to the table,” said Marfell.

“Jennifer has a truly global palate and a sharp sense of how Marlborough wines sit on the international stage, and Terry has been judging here and overseas for more than 30 years. Their perspective alongside the deep local knowledge of our panel is exactly the balance a regional show needs.”

Jennifer Docherty is one of around 420 Masters of Wine worldwide, and the first ethnically Chinese and Mandarin-speaking MW. Based in Hong Kong, she has spent more than 16 years as a wine buyer and educator across the UK, Hong Kong and mainland China. She now works as an educator, a judge and a wine communicator who has chaired a judging panel at the IWC Sake Competition in London for a decade.

Terry Copeland has judged wine competitions for more than three decades across New Zealand, London, San Francisco, Sydney and Tokyo. After a career in wine sales, marketing, export and supply chain, he went on to lead NZ Young Farmers and Federated Farmers, and is now Programme Director, Export Growth at the Ministry for Primary Industries.

Organisers said entries cover the full range of Marlborough wine styles, with growth in several classes this year. Sweet wine entries have almost doubled, the Sauvignon Blanc aged one year or older category is up and so is the current vintage regional blend Pinot Noir.

“It’s great to see more aged Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir coming through,” Marfell said.

“These styles work to showcase the depth and breadth Marlborough has to offer, as well as the confidence producers have in how their wines develop over time.”

The Legacy Trophy, which awards the wine with the highest scores for three vintages within a ten-year period, will be judged solely by the chief judges and guest judges today (20 October), before judging gets into full swing tomorrow.

QuayConnect is once again the show’s naming sponsor with general manager Jaron McLeod saying the company is proud to continue its support.

“Marlborough wine is one of the top of the south’s great export stories, and much of it moves through our supply chain on its way to the world,” he said.

“Backing a show that recognises the skill and care that goes into every bottle is a natural fit for QuayConnect.”

Entrants will be notified of medal results on Thursday 29 October, with trophy winners announced at the Marlborough Wine Show Celebration on Friday 13 November 2026.

content:
The winery castle at All Saints Estate. Image credit Griffin Simm

KIN Restaurant at All Saints Estate has been awarded a Chef’s Hat in The Age Good Food Guide 2027, its third hat since opening in January 2023, with a score of 15/20.

Described by the guide as having “dishes shaped by a restless creativity”, the award recognises KIN’s “commitment to regional produce, quality and exceptional dining”.

Set within the heritage listed 19th-century castle at All Saints Estate on the banks of the Murray River, KIN is led by executive chef Jack Cassidy.

His menus showcase seasonal produce from local growers and the estate’s own gardens and vineyards, with an “inventive use of native ingredients, matched with wines from All Saints Estate, St Leonards Vineyard and Mount Ophir Estate”.

Owners said the hat reaffirms KIN as one of Australia’s destination dining venues and that its setting within a winery is what makes it unique.

“Nick, Angela and I are incredibly proud to see KIN awarded a hat in The Age Good Food Guide 2027. It’s wonderful recognition for Jack and the team, who create dishes that reflect the seasons, our gardens and our connection to the region,” said Eliza Brown, director at All Saints Estate.

“This award would not be possible without our loyal guests and the hard work, passion and creativity of our team.”

Cassidy said the recognition is “for the team”.

Every day we work with what the region and our own gardens give us, and to have that recognised by The Age Good Food Guide means a great deal to every one of us,” he said.

First published in 1979, The Age Good Food Guide “remains the benchmark for dining in Victoria”.
